reason: The sources provide rich, verified details across multiple sites on the theoretical discovery, internal physics, candidate stars, and violent life cycle of Thorne–Żytkow objects.
story: In 1977, physicists Kip Thorne and Anna Żytkow calculated the physics of a cosmic monster: a dead, city-sized neutron star swallowed whole by a living red supergiant. Known as a Thorne–Żytkow object (TŻO), this hybrid star is born when a binary companion expands or suffers a supernova kick, dragging the ultra-dense neutron star into its core. Inside, the dead star’s crushing gravity funnels surrounding gas onto its surface at near-light speed, reaching temperatures approaching one billion Kelvin. This furnace acts as a cosmic blender, powering interrupted rapid proton capture that synthesizes bizarre overabundances of rubidium, molybdenum, and lithium before convective currents blast them to the surface. To outside telescopes, a TŻO masquerades as an ordinary red supergiant. In 2014, astronomers found a strong candidate named HV 2112 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, though its nature remains fiercely debated before the monster inevitably collapses into a black hole.
angle: Deep inside what looks like an ordinary red supergiant star, a dead neutron star sits at the center, devouring its host from the inside out and turning it into a heavy-metal factory.

claims.claim: Thorne–Żytkow objects were first theoretically hypothesized by Kip Thorne and Anna Żytkow in the 1970s.
A Thorne–Żytkow object is a hybrid star consisting of a red giant or supergiant containing a degenerate neutron star at its core.
The hybrid star can form in a binary system when an expanding companion star engulfs a neutron star in a common-envelope phase.
Dynamical drag and friction against the gas envelope cause the neutron star to spiral inward toward the center.
Asymmetric supernova kicks can alter a newborn neutron star's trajectory to collide with or merge into its stellar companion.
Thorne–Żytkow objects can also form through direct physical collisions between wandering stars in dense globular star clusters.
Gas falling onto the neutron star core heats up to extreme temperatures approaching one billion Kelvin.
The extreme temperatures at the core boundary drive rapid proton-capture nucleosynthesis (rp-process).
Internal convection pumps distinctive chemical overabundances of lithium, rubidium, and molybdenum to the outer atmosphere.
From the outside, a Thorne–Żytkow object visually resembles an ordinary cool red supergiant star.
A Thorne–Żytkow object has a relatively short theoretical lifespan estimated between 100,000 and 1,000,000 years.
Between 10 and 200 Thorne–Żytkow objects are estimated to exist in the Milky Way at any given time.
In 2014, a team led by astronomer Emily Levesque proposed the star HV 2112 as the first observed candidate.
Candidate star HV 2112 is located in the Small Magellanic Cloud.
The classification of HV 2112 as a true Thorne–Żytkow object remains contested and subject to debate among astronomers.
As the neutron star core accretes matter, it can exceed the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit and collapse into a black hole.
Strong winds or envelope mass loss can strip the outer layers away to reveal a neutron star or isolated pulsar with an accretion disk.
Gravitational-wave observatories like LIGO could detect continuous waves emitted by the inner neutron star core of a Thorne–Żytkow object.

disputed: Whether candidate star HV 2112 is a genuine Thorne–Żytkow object: Emily Levesque's team proposed it based on lithium, rubidium, and molybdenum detections, but later research disputed this, arguing its luminosity is too low and that a super-asymptotic giant branch star could mimic the chemistry. A script should attribute this as an unconfirmed candidate under ongoing debate.

The final fate of a Thorne–Żytkow object: sources describe both catastrophic collapse into a black hole and complete envelope expulsion leaving behind a neutron star, pulsar, or magnetar. A script should frame these as alternative theoretical outcomes.
